title: China drafts cyberbullying rules that reach AI-generated abuse
excerpt: China’s internet regulator has published draft rules to combat cyberbullying, and, according to Reuters, the measures are written to reach abuse generated with artificial intelligence. The Cyberspace Administration of China released the draft for public comment on 29 July, part of a widening effort to police what happens on the country’s platforms. The draft targets […]
content_html:
China’s internet regulator has published draft rules to combat cyberbullying, and, according to Reuters, the measures are written to reach abuse generated with artificial intelligence.

The Cyberspace Administration of China released the draft for public comment on 29 July, part of a widening effort to police what happens on the country’s platforms.

The draft targets what Chinese regulators call “cyberviolence.” That covers the online spread of harassing, defamatory, or false information that harms a person, a category the regulator defines broadly enough to fold in AI misuse alongside ordinary trolling and pile-ons.

Most of the weight falls on platforms. Under the draft, services would have to build classifiers that detect cyberviolence, offer users a “one-click protection” that blocks incoming messages and comments, and act on those signals by restricting abusive content and investigating the accounts behind it.

The enforcement machinery is detailed. Platforms would keep blacklists of repeat offenders, file regular reports on their interventions, and run early-warning systems to catch pile-ons before they escalate, with penalties running up to the closure of an abuser’s account.

Some platforms are already moving ahead of the text. The question-and-answer site Zhihu, anticipating the rules, has moved to curb anonymous accounts, a sign of how quickly Chinese companies adjust once a regulatory direction becomes clear.

The AI dimension is what makes it timely. Reuters reports that the rules are meant to cover AI-enabled abuse, the deepfaked images and synthetic text that can be produced at volume and aimed at a single target, a form of harassment that older moderation systems were never built to catch.

It fits a pattern of Chinese AI rulemaking. Beijing already requires AI-generated content to be labelled and has moved to regulate human-like AI services and a digital-human industry in which people even rent out their faces to AI, building a lattice of rules that treats synthetic media as something to be tracked rather than left alone.

The state’s interest is not only protective. The same tools that detect abuse also identify speakers, and a regime that requires platforms to log, trace, and blacklist users hands the authorities a fuller map of who is saying what, a point critics of China’s internet governance make repeatedly.

That tension runs through the draft. Framed as a shield for victims of harassment, it also deepens the obligations that make Chinese platforms answerable to the state, and the line between protecting users and surveilling them is, as ever, drawn by the government.

The victims it names are real enough. Cyberbullying campaigns in China have driven people offline and, in some cases, to worse, and public anger after several high-profile cases has given the authorities a popular mandate to act.

Anonymity sits at the centre of the fight. Much online abuse in China is posted from anonymous or pseudonymous accounts, and the draft’s logging and blacklist requirements press platforms to know who is behind them, which is exactly what makes the rules effective and what makes them worrying.

Other governments are circling the same problem. From deepfake abuse to synthetic harassment, regulators from Europe to the United States are trying to write rules for AI-generated cruelty, and China’s draft is among the more prescriptive attempts so far.

What happens next is procedural. The draft is open for public comment before it can be finalised, and the details that matter, how aggressively platforms must scan and how precisely the AI provisions are worded, may shift before the rules take effect.

The direction, though, is set. China is building the plumbing to detect and act on AI-generated abuse at scale, and whatever the final text says, the expectation it sets for platforms is that they will see everything, and answer for it.

content_html_zh:
中国互联网监管机构发布了打击网络欺凌的规则草案，据路透社报道，这些措施旨在解决人工智能产生的滥用行为。

中国国家互联网信息办公室于 7 月 29 日发布了草案征求公众意见，这是监管国家平台上发生的事情的广泛努力的一部分。

该草案针对的是中国监管机构所称的“网络暴力”。 这涵盖了网上传播伤害他人的骚扰、诽谤或虚假信息的行为，监管机构对这一类别的定义非常广泛，足以将人工智能滥用与普通的恶意攻击和恶意攻击并列在一起。

大部分重量落在平台上。 根据该草案，服务必须建立检测网络暴力的分类器，为用户提供“一键式保护”来阻止传入的消息和评论，并通过限制滥用内容和调查其背后的帐户来对这些信号采取行动。

执法机制很详细。 平台将保留惯犯的黑名单，定期提交有关干预措施的报告，并运行预警系统，在问题升级之前发现它们，处罚直至关闭滥用者的账户。

欧盟科技的💜

来自欧盟科技界的最新传言、我们明智的创始人鲍里斯的故事，以及一些值得怀疑的人工智能艺术。 每周都会免费发送到您的收件箱中。 立即注册！

一些平台已经领先于文本。 问答网站知乎预见到了这些规定，已采取行动限制匿名账户，这表明一旦监管方向明确，中国企业的调整速度有多快。

人工智能维度使其变得及时。 路透社报道称，这些规则旨在涵盖人工智能滥用、可大量生成并针对单一目标的深度伪造图像和合成文本，这是旧版审核系统无法捕捉到的一种骚扰形式。

它符合中国人工智能规则制定的模式。 北京已经要求对人工智能生成的内容进行标记，并开始监管类人人工智能服务和数字人类产业，在这个产业中，人们甚至将自己的脸出租给人工智能，建立了一套规则，将合成媒体视为可追踪的东西，而不是单独处理。

国家利益不仅仅是保护性的。 检测滥用行为的工具还可以识别说话者，而要求平台记录、追踪用户并将用户列入黑名单的制度，可以让当局更全面地了解谁在说什么，这是中国互联网治理批评者反复提出的观点。

这种紧张气氛贯穿整个选秀。 它被视为骚扰受害者的盾牌，也加深了中国平台对国家负责的义务，保护用户和监视用户之间的界限一如既往地由政府划定。

它所提到的受害者是足够真实的。 中国的网络欺凌活动导致人们失去联系，在某些情况下甚至变得更糟，在几起备受瞩目的案件发生后，公众的愤怒让当局普遍授权采取行动。

匿名是这场斗争的核心。 中国的许多网络滥用行为都是通过匿名或假名账户发布的，草案的记录和黑名单要求平台了解谁是幕后黑手，这正是这些规则有效的原因，也是令人担忧的原因。

其他政府也在考虑同样的问题。 从深度伪造滥用到合成骚扰，从欧洲到美国的监管机构都在试图为人工智能产生的残酷行为制定规则，而中国的草案是迄今为止更具规范性的尝试之一。

接下来发生的事情是程序性的。 该草案在最终定稿之前正在征求公众意见，而重要的细节，例如平台必须如何积极地进行扫描以及人工智能条款的措辞如何精确，可能会在规则生效之前发生变化。

但方向已经确定。 中国正在建立管道，以大规模检测人工智能产生的滥用行为并采取行动，无论最终文本如何，它对平台的期望是它们将看到一切，并对此负责。
